questions.q: What is REST?
questions.explain: REST is not something you install. It is a way of designing an API: URLs name resources, methods are the verbs, and the body carries a representation. Follow the habits and developers can guess how your API works.
options: A library you install with npm to build HTTP servers
A style for designing HTTP APIs: a set of habits that make an API predictable
A binary data format that replaces JSON
A new version of the HTTP protocol

questions.q: Which request deletes task 7 in REST style?
questions.explain: The item URL is /tasks/7, and the method DELETE is the verb. A GET must never change data, so ?action=delete is the worst choice of all.

questions.q: An old API has POST /tasks/7/markDone. What is the REST way to mark task 7 as done?
questions.explain: Marking a task done changes one field of an existing resource, which is exactly what PATCH is for. The URL stays the plain item URL.

questions.q: A client sends POST /tasks and the task is created. What should the success response be?
questions.explain: 201 Created says a new resource exists. The body returns it (with its new id), and Location gives its URL, for example /tasks/8.
options: 201 with the new task and a Location header

questions.q: What does a successful DELETE /tasks/7 usually return?
questions.explain: 204 No Content means "it worked, and there is nothing to send back". 404 is for a task that did not exist when the request arrived.
options: 200 with the deleted task's id as text
404, because the task is now gone

questions.q: What is the difference between PUT /tasks/7 and PATCH /tasks/7?
questions.explain: With PUT you send the complete new representation. With PATCH you send only what changes, such as {"done": true}.
options: PUT creates a new task; PATCH deletes it
PUT replaces the whole task; PATCH changes only the fields you send
They are the same; PATCH is just the newer name
PATCH replaces the whole task; PUT changes one field

questions.q: Which URL follows the naming habits from the lesson?
questions.explain: Use plural nouns, lower case, and hyphens between words. /getTaskLists also hides a verb in the URL.

questions.q: Comment 2 belongs to task 7, which belongs to project 3. Task 7 has its own id. Which URL does the lesson recommend for the task's comments?
questions.explain: Nest at most one level. Once a task has its own id, address it directly as /tasks/7; the project is not needed in the URL.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say to write the API contract before writing code?
questions.explain: The contract (URLs, bodies, status codes) is a promise. Web apps, mobile apps and other teams depend on it, so decide it carefully up front.
options: Because Node.js refuses to start a server without one
Clients build against the contract, so changing it later breaks them
Because a contract makes the server run faster
Because the contract replaces the need for tests

questions.q: Why should a list endpoint return {"data": [...], "meta": {...}} instead of a bare array?
questions.explain: A bare array has nowhere to put extra information. With an object, adding meta.total or a cursor later is an additive change that old clients simply ignore.
options: JSON cannot contain an array at the top level
A wrapped list is smaller to send
It leaves room to add fields such as the total count later without breaking clients
Browsers cannot parse bare arrays with fetch

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every query value arrives as a string, so "false" is not the boolean false. A missing parameter gives null, not undefined.
questions.code:
const params = new URLSearchParams("limit=5&done=false");
console.log(typeof params.get("limit"), params.get("done") === false, params.get("sort"));

questions.q: A client sends ?limit= with nothing after the equals sign. What does this print?
questions.explain: The parameter is present, with the empty string as its value. Number("") is 0, which is below the minimum of 1, so a range check rejects it.

questions.q: This is the check the lesson uses for limit. What does it print?
questions.explain: Number.isInteger is false for 2.5 and for NaN (from "abc"). 500 is a whole number but above the maximum of 100.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The regular expression /^-/ removes a minus sign only at the start. The leading minus is the usual way to ask for descending order.

questions.q: A client sends ?sort=password. Why must the server check the field against an allow-list?
questions.explain: Never sort by whatever the client sends. An allow-list such as ["id", "title", "createdAt"] keeps private columns out of reach and turns anything else into a clear 400.
options: Because URLSearchParams cannot read the word password
Sorting by any field the client names can leak or probe hidden data and break queries; only listed fields are safe
Because sorting is only allowed on numbers
It is not needed; the database ignores unknown fields

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both the search text and each title are lowered before comparing, so the search ignores upper and lower case and finds both tasks.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: total counts every match (three open tasks), not just the ones on this page. That lets the client know more pages exist.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Dates in the form YYYY-MM-DD compare correctly as strings. Flipping the sign of order gives newest first: 09-03, 09-02, 09-01.

questions.q: Two tasks have the same createdAt. When you sort by createdAt in SQL, what should you add?
questions.explain: toSorted keeps equal items in their original order, but a database gives no such promise. Without a tie-breaker, equal rows can swap places between pages.
options: Nothing; databases always keep equal rows in insert order
A tie-breaker, such as the id, so the order is the same every time
A random number, so every client sees a fair order

questions.q: With ?limit=3&offset=3, which items are sent?
questions.explain: Offset means "skip this many": skip 3 (a, b, c), then take 3. slice stops before its end index.

questions.q: A client reads the newest items, two per page. Between page 1 and page 2, item 5 is deleted. What does this print?
questions.explain: After the delete, everything shifts one place forward. Item 4 moved to position 1, which was already read, so the client never sees it. Offset pagination can skip or repeat items when data changes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: btoa turns text into Base64 and atob turns it back. The cursor is the same one the lesson's server produced for "ids smaller than 5".

questions.q: Why does the lesson encode the cursor with Base64 instead of sending {"before": 5} as plain JSON?
questions.explain: Base64 is not encryption: anyone can decode it. It only signals "do not look inside". The server must still validate every cursor it receives.
options: Base64 encrypts the cursor, so clients cannot read it
So clients treat it as an opaque token and send it back, instead of building their own
Because JSON cannot be put in a query string
Because Base64 makes the response smaller

questions.q: This is the lesson's cursor decoder. What does it print?
questions.explain: A cursor comes from the client, so it is untrusted input. Bad Base64 or bad JSON throws and is caught; a before that is not a whole number is rejected too. Either way the server answers with a 400.

questions.q: This cursor page reads "ids smaller than before". Task 8 arrives between the two pages. What does this print?
questions.explain: The cursor remembers where page 1 ended (id 5), not how many items to skip. The new task 8 is larger than 5, so it cannot push anything onto page 2 twice.

questions.q: A mobile app has an activity feed with infinite scroll. New activity arrives all the time. Which pagination fits best?
questions.explain: The user only scrolls forward and data changes constantly. A cursor never repeats or skips items when new ones arrive.
options: No pagination; send the whole feed
Offset pagination with a very large limit

questions.q: What media type does an RFC 9457 problem details response use?
questions.explain: application/problem+json tells the client from the header alone that the body is a problem details object.

questions.q: Which problem details field is a URL that names the kind of problem, so clients can compare it in code?
questions.explain: type never changes for a given kind of problem, so it is safe to compare. title is for humans, and detail describes this one occurrence.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type is built into a full URL. With no extra, the object has four keys: type, title, status and detail.

questions.q: A database query fails inside GET /v1/tasks. What belongs in the problem details detail sent to the client?
questions.explain: Attackers read error messages too. Stack traces, SQL and file paths reveal how your server is built. Log them on the server and send a plain message.
options: The full stack trace, so the client can report it
The SQL query that failed, so the client can fix it
A short safe message; the stack trace and SQL go only to the server log
The internal file path and line number of the error

questions.q: Which change is a breaking change that needs a new API version?
questions.explain: Renaming or removing a field makes working clients fail, because they still read done. The other three are additive: old clients keep working.
options: Adding a new optional query parameter since
Adding a new field priority to each task in responses

questions.q: What is the most common way to version a REST API, as used in the lesson?
questions.explain: A path version is visible in every log line and easy to route. Some APIs use a header such as Accept-Version: 2 instead.
options: A version number in the JSON body of each request
A version in the path, such as /v1/tasks
A different port for each version
A new domain name for each version

questions.q: The server adds a Link header when more items exist. What does this print?
questions.explain: searchParams.set adds offset=2 and keeps the other parameters. The client gets the exact URL of the next page, so it does not have to compute it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: pathname is only the path, without the query string. The server routes on the path and reads options from searchParams.
questions.code:
const url = new URL("/v1/tasks?sort=-title&q=milk", "http://localhost");
console.log(url.pathname, url.searchParams.get("sort"), url.searchParams.get("limit"));

questions.q: Finish parseSort. It takes the sort text (or null when missing) and returns { field, desc }. A missing sort means { field: "id", desc: false }. A leading - means descending. If the field is not in SORTABLE, return null.
questions.explain: Default with ??, strip one leading minus with /^-/, then check the allow-list. A field like password is refused no matter what.

questions.q: Finish paginate for offset pagination. Return { data, meta }, where data is the page of items and meta is { total, limit, offset } with total being the number of all items.
questions.explain: slice(offset, offset + limit) skips offset items and takes up to limit. The last page can be shorter. total is all items, not the page length.
questions.expected:
{ data: [ 'a', 'b' ], meta: { total: 5, limit: 2, offset: 0 } }
{ data: [ 'e' ], meta: { total: 5, limit: 2, offset: 4 } }

questions.q: Finish parseLimit. It gets a URLSearchParams. If limit is missing, return 20. If it is a whole number from 1 to 100, return it as a number. Otherwise return the string "invalid".
questions.explain: Check has first for the default. Then convert with Number and use Number.isInteger, which rejects both NaN and decimals, before the range check.
questions.expected:
(none) 20
limit=5 5
limit=0 invalid
limit=2.5 invalid
limit=abc invalid
limit=100 100

questions.q: Finish filterByDone. done is the raw query text: "true", "false" or null. null means no filter. Return the ids of the matching tasks.
questions.explain: The query value is a string, so compare it with "true" to get a real boolean. Boolean("false") would be true, a classic bug.

questions.q: Finish problem so it returns an RFC 9457 problem details object with type (as https://example.com/problems/ plus the given name), title, status, detail, and any extra fields. The program prints it as JSON.
questions.explain: Build the object in the order type, title, status, detail, then spread extra to add your own fields such as errors.

questions.q: Finish page(limit, before) for cursor pagination over ids, newest first. Return { data, next }: data holds up to limit ids smaller than before, and next is the last id in data when more ids remain, otherwise null. Tip: take limit + 1 ids.
questions.explain: Take one row more than needed. If it exists, there is a next page, and the cursor is the last id actually sent. On the last page next is null.
questions.expected: { data: [ 7, 6, 5 ], next: 5 } { data: [ 4, 3, 2 ], next: 2 } { data: [ 1 ], next: null }

questions.q: Finish operation(method, path). It returns the CRUD name for a REST request on /tasks: "list", "create", "read", "update" (for PATCH) or "delete". Anything else returns "unknown". An item path looks like /tasks/7 (digits only).
questions.explain: Two URL shapes (collection and item) and a handful of methods cover all of CRUD. A verb in the URL, like /tasks/7/delete, does not fit the pattern.
questions.expected:
list create read
update delete unknown

questions.q: Finish removedFields(oldTask, newTask). It returns the names of fields that exist in oldTask but not in newTask. Removed or renamed fields are breaking changes; new fields are not.
questions.explain: Adding priority removes nothing, so it is additive. Renaming done to completed removes done, which breaks every client that reads it: that needs /v2.

questions.q: Finish nextLink(path, limit, offset, total). When more items exist after this page, return the next page's URL as path?limit=…&offset=…. On the last page return null.
questions.explain: The next page starts at offset + limit. When that is already at or past total, there is nothing left, so there is no next link. The server does this math so the client does not have to.
